tagline: An early automobile route survives in Ohio’s old highway streets.
intro: Ohio’s Lincoln Highway Historic Byway follows a road whose older town streets and later numbered alignments tell different chapters of automobile travel. At Cairo, the old route crosses flat farming country as Main Street, while US 30 runs south of town. Ohio DOT recognizes the Lincoln Highway in its byways program for its place in the growth of automobile culture. At East Liverpool, present US 30 is a four-lane divided highway with limited access beside the Ohio River.

Carl G. Fisher conceived the coast-to-coast highway in 1912; the Lincoln Highway Association formed the following year to plan, promote and sign it. Dedicated in October 1913, it linked Times Square with San Francisco’s Lincoln Park. Less than half the selected route had an improved surface. The association’s early private-financing ambition gave way to promotion and lobbying for government construction. Numbered highways followed in 1926, with much of the Lincoln route becoming US 30.

Travel east from Gomer to Cairo on the old Lincoln route. Farther east, Massillon and Lisbon retain Lincoln Way or Lincolnway street names. At East Liverpool, the journey reaches the Ohio River and a city shaped by pottery. Here US 30 crosses into West Virginia on the Jennings Randolph Bridge.

moments.title: Gomer
moments.text: An Antarctic expedition vehicle came to grief on the Lincoln Highway at Gomer before it ever reached the ice. On October 28, 1939, Admiral Richard E. Byrd’s Snow Cruiser ran off a small bridge into a stream after its steering was damaged. It was traveling from the Chicago area to the Boston Army Wharf and remained at Gomer for three days. The machine continued to Antarctica, where its smooth tires failed to grip the ice. Gomer stands at Gomer Road and the Old Lincoln Highway, north of present US 30.

moments.title: Cairo
moments.text: Cairo’s Main Street once carried US 30 and the Lincoln Highway through the middle of farming country. In the 1970s, an upgraded US 30 moved approximately one mile south, leaving the old east-west route as the village’s Main Street. The community was platted as West Cairo in 1848; its post office dropped “West” from the name in 1922. The old road continues toward Beaverdam to the east, while Gomer lies to the west. The land is generally flat and moderately wooded, with Rattlesnake Creek passing just west of the village.

moments.title: East Liverpool
moments.text: East Liverpool’s pottery industry began in 1839 when English potter James Bennett established production using local clay and good transport connections. Potters from Staffordshire followed, attracted by higher wages and the prospect of owning land. By 1879 the city had 24 potteries, nearly all run by English immigrants. The Museum of Ceramics displays Lotus Ware, an ornamental porcelain made by Knowles, Taylor & Knowles in the 1890s. The Ohio River borders the city, and US 30 crosses it on the Jennings Randolph Bridge. Its decoration drew on Moorish and Persian designs; the porcelain earned recognition at Chicago’s 1893 World’s Columbian Exposition.
